title: Speech into mind, mind into the self
theme: The wise one should hold speech in the mind, the mind in the knowing self, the knowing self in the great self, and that in the peaceful self.

words.context: Śaṅkara: «वाक् वाचम्», and speech stands for all the senses; Raṅgarāmānuja, quoting the Bhāṣyakāra: the accusative ending is dropped

words.role: place into which speech is held
object of the second yacchet: the mind

words.context: Śaṅkara: «ज्ञाने प्रकाशस्वरूपे बुद्धावात्मनि», in the intellect, whose nature is light

words.role: object of the fourth yacchet: the great self
words.context: Raṅgarāmānuja (quoting the Bhāṣyakāra): neuter by exchange of gender, «व्यत्ययेन तदिति नपुंसकलिङ्गता»

sandhi.type: t before a voiced consonant; k before a nasal
sandhi.rule: The final t becomes d before v, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते); the final k becomes the nasal ṅ before m, P. 8.4.45 (यरोऽनुनासिकेऽनुनासिको वा).
The visarga becomes s before t, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः).

sandhi.type: t before j; e before a vowel
sandhi.rule: The final t becomes j before j, P. 8.4.40 (स्तोः श्चुना श्चुः); the e of jñāne becomes ay before ā and the y is dropped, P. 6.1.78 (एचोऽयवायावः) with P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य), leaving the hiatus jñāna ātmani.

sandhi.type: t before ś; e before a vowel
sandhi.rule: The final t becomes c before ś, P. 8.4.40 (स्तोः श्चुना श्चुः), and the ś may become ch, P. 8.4.63 (शश्छोऽटि); śānte becomes śānta before ātmani as above.

morphology.note: Both commentators read vāk as the accusative vācam with its ending dropped. Raṅgarāmānuja, quoting the Bhāṣyakāra, cites P. 7.1.39 (सुपां सुलुक्पूर्वसवर्णाऽऽच्छेयाडाड्यायाजालः) for the dropping. Read as one word, vāṅmanasī would be a dual dvandva ‘speech and mind’; neither commentary takes it so.
For the locative manasi, with the final i lengthened — a Vedic licence, as Śaṅkara («छान्दसं दैर्घ्यम्») and Raṅgarāmānuja («सप्तम्याश्छान्दसो दीर्घः») both say. Madhva's text reads manasi.
The second tat stands for the great self (masculine) but is neuter; Raṅgarāmānuja calls this an exchange of gender, a Vedic licence.

translation.literal: The wise one should hold speech in the mind; that [mind] he should hold in the knowing self; the knowing he should hold down in the great self; that he should hold in the peaceful self.
translation.readable: Let the wise one draw speech into the mind, the mind into the knowing self, the knowing self into the great self, and that into the self at peace.

anvaya: प्राज्ञः वाक् मनसी यच्छेत्, तत् ज्ञाने आत्मनि यच्छेत्, ज्ञानम् महति आत्मनि नियच्छेत्, तत् शान्ते आत्मनि यच्छेत् ।
syntax: Four optative clauses with one subject, prājñaḥ. Each has an accusative (what is held) and a locative (where it is held); each locative becomes the next accusative, so the sentence climbs the ladder of 1.3.10–11 in reverse, from outer to inner.

ambiguities.note: Both commentators divide vāk + manasī: speech (accusative, ending dropped) into the mind (locative, lengthened). A reading as one word, ‘speech and mind’ (dual), would make speech and mind together the object; neither commentary adopts it, and Madhva's text reads manasi.

Śaṅkara: the mind into the intellect, the intellect into the first-born Hiraṇyagarbha, that into the peaceful self, «शान्ते सर्वविशेषप्रत्यस्तमितरूपे अविक्रिये सर्वान्तरे सर्वबुद्धिप्रत्ययसाक्षिणि मुख्ये आत्मनि». Raṅgarāmānuja, quoting the Bhāṣyakāra: the mind into the intellect, the intellect into the individual self as agent, and that self into the supreme Brahman, «परस्मिन् ब्रह्मणि सर्वान्तर्यामिणि नियच्छेत्». Madhva reads a hierarchy of deities, each held in the one above.

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: Counted as written, 16 and 19 syllables: the last pāda, niyacchet tad yacchec chānta ātmani, has eleven. Madhva's text lacks tad yacchet there, which gives eight (corrections.json).

beginner: This verse gives a practice. The previous verse said the self is hidden and seen only by a fine, steady mind. Here is how such a mind is made: step by step, from the outside in. First, let speech settle into the mind: stop talking, outwardly and then inwardly. Then let the mind settle into the part of us that knows and decides. Let that settle into the great self, and let that come to rest in the self that is at peace. The steps are the same ladder as a few verses earlier, climbed back down from the outside toward the inside. Śaṅkara takes speech as standing for all the senses, and the peaceful self as the inmost Self, the witness of every thought. Raṅgarāmānuja takes the last step as resting the individual self in the Lord who dwells within it.
analogy: Like closing a set of nested doors from the outermost inward, until one stands in the quiet inner room.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It gives four steps of restraint, each held in the next: speech in the mind, the mind in the knowing self, the knowing self in the great self, and that in the peaceful self.

commentary.q: Śaṅkara: the means of reaching it
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The verse gives the means to the knowledge of 1.3.12: «तत्प्रतिपत्त्युपायमाह». Speech stands for all the senses, «वागत्रोपलक्षणार्था सर्वेषामिन्द्रियाणाम्». The mind is held in the intellect, «ज्ञाने प्रकाशस्वरूपे बुद्धावात्मनि»; the intellect in the first-born, «आत्मनि महति प्रथमजे»; and that in the peaceful Self, without any distinction or change, the witness of every thought.

commentary.q: Raṅgarāmānuja: the practice of inward yoga
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: He reads the verse as the practice promised by ‘inward yoga’ in 1.2.12: «'अध्यात्मयोगाधिगमेन' इति निर्दिष्ट जीवस्वरूपज्ञानप्रकारं दर्शयति». Quoting the Bhāṣyakāra, the last step holds the individual self as agent in the supreme Brahman, the inner controller of all, «परस्मिन् ब्रह्मणि सर्वान्तर्यामिणि नियच्छेत्», and the chariot so driven is to reach Viṣṇu's place. He then reports a work he names, the Śrutaprakāśikā, on what each step means, and defends the Bhāṣyakāra's grammar against an objection.

commentary.q: Madhva: restraint as meditation on dependence
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: His comment holds each deity in the one above, up to Viṣṇu: «तौ रमायां परानन्दे तां विष्णौ परमात्मनि». Restraint, it says, is nothing but meditating on each as dependent on the one above: «तद्वशत्वेन तद्ध्यानं नियमो नाम नापरः». A verse he cites («इति च») asks how a man could restrain the gods who restrain him: «कुतस्तु मानुषो देवान्नियच्छेद्विनियामकान्».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: Both read vāk as an accusative without its ending and manasī as a Vedic locative: Śaṅkara, «छान्दसं दैर्घ्यम्»; Raṅgarāmānuja, quoting the Bhāṣyakāra, «सप्तम्याश्छान्दसो दीर्घः». The extra tad yacchet makes the last pāda eleven syllables; Madhva's text lacks it.

advaita.text: The senses are withdrawn into the mind, the mind into the intellect, the intellect into Hiraṇyagarbha, and that into the peaceful Self, the witness of all thought: «सर्वबुद्धिप्रत्ययसाक्षिणि मुख्ये आत्मनि».

visistadvaita.text: The practice of inward yoga, ending with the individual self held in the supreme Brahman, the inner controller: «परस्मिन् ब्रह्मणि सर्वान्तर्यामिणि नियच्छेत्».

dvaita.text: Each presiding deity is held in the one above, up to Viṣṇu, and restraint is meditation on that dependence: «तद्वशत्वेन तद्ध्यानं नियमो नाम नापरः».

schools.disagreement: Whether the last step dissolves all into the one peaceful Self (Śaṅkara), rests the individual self in the Lord within it (Raṅgarāmānuja), or is meditation on a hierarchy of dependent deities up to Viṣṇu (Madhva).

parallels.quote: आत्मसंस्थं मनः कृत्वा न किञ्चिदपि चिन्तयेत्
parallels.note: The Gītā describes the same gradual stilling: the mind made to rest in the self.

parallels.quote: वैष्णवस्य परमपदस्य दुरवगमत्वमुक्त्वा तदवगमार्थं योगं दर्शयति
parallels.note: In the Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya Śaṅkara reads this verse as the yoga the text gives for reaching Viṣṇu's highest place, after saying in 1.3.12 how hard it is to know; he glosses the first words as ‘let him hold speech in the mind’ (vācaṃ manasi saṃyacchet).

contemporary.text: The verse describes settling the mind as a sequence rather than a single act: first stop speaking, then let thinking slow, then let deciding rest. People who try to silence the mind all at once often find this kind of stepwise approach easier. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: Which is easier for you to quiet: your speech, your thoughts, or your decisions?
reflect.deeper: The verse runs the ladder of 1.3.10–11 from the outside in. Why might the way back be described as restraint rather than as climbing?
reflect.practice: Sit for five minutes. First stop speaking aloud, then notice inner speech and let it slow; do not force it.

references.text: Raṅgarāmānuja quotes the Bhāṣyakāra (in his school, Rāmānuja) and a work he names, the Śrutaprakāśikā; these are reported as cited by him. Madhva's comment on 1.3.12–13 is one passage after 1.3.13 and concerns this verse.

flags.note: Madhva's text reads vāṅmanasi (short i) and lacks tad yacchet in the last line (corrections.json).
The four places of restraint, and whether the last is the peaceful Self itself (Śaṅkara), the Lord within the self (Raṅgarāmānuja) or Viṣṇu at the head of a hierarchy of deities (Madhva).
